docs.compound: The passato prossimo is formed with the present of avere or essere plus the past participle. Participle endings: -are → -ato (parlato), -ere → -uto (venduto), -ire → -ito (dormito); with essere, the participle agrees in gender and number with the subject (lei è andata).

groups.name: Verbs in -are (1st conjugation)
groups.note: Drop -are from the infinitive to get the stem (parl-) and add the endings; in the future, -are changes to -er- (parler-).

groups.name: Verbs in -ere (2nd conjugation)
groups.note: Drop -ere to get the stem (vend-) and add the endings; the future keeps the vowel e (venderò).

groups.example: dormire – to sleep (and finire – to finish, which adds -isc-)
groups.name: Verbs in -ire (3rd conjugation)
groups.note: Drop -ire to get the stem (dorm-); many verbs like finire insert -isc- in the io, tu, lui/lei and loro present forms (finisco, finisci, finisce, finiscono).

irregular.de: to know (a fact), to know how

tips: Learn the noi form first: it is always regular in the present (-iamo) and a useful anchor for the stem.
Subject pronouns are usually dropped because the ending already shows the person: 'parlo' means 'I speak'.
Memorize the irregular participles together with the verb, especially fare–fatto, dire–detto, vedere–visto and essere–stato.

rules: Vowels are pure and short (a, e, i, o, u); never glide them as English does.
C and G are soft (like 'ch' and 'j') before e/i, and hard (like 'k' and 'g') before a/o/u; 'ch' and 'gh' make them hard before e/i.
Double consonants are held longer: 'pala' (shovel) vs 'palla' (ball).
Stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable; a written accent marks final-syllable stress (città).
topics.summary: Italian is largely phonetic: words are pronounced as they are written. Learn the vowel sounds, double consonants and the soft/hard c and g.
topics.tip: English speakers often say 'pizza' as 'peet-sa' correctly but then say 'bruschetta' with 'sh'; remember 'sch' before e is 'sk': brus-KET-ta.
topics.title: Pronunciation & Stress

rules: Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine and those ending in -a usually feminine; -e can be either.
Definite articles ('the'): il/lo/l' (masc.), la/l' (fem.); use lo before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, and l' before vowels.
Indefinite articles ('a'): un/uno (masc.), una/un' (fem.).
Gender must be learned with the noun, so learn 'il libro', not just 'libro'.
topics.summary: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, and the article (the word for 'a' or 'the') must match it.
topics.tip: Watch exceptions like 'il problema' and 'il turista' (masculine despite -a).
topics.title: Nouns, Gender & Articles

rules: Masculine -o becomes -i; feminine -a becomes -e; -e becomes -i.
Articles change too: il→i, lo/l'→gli, la→le.
Words ending in an accented vowel or in a consonant (foreign words) stay unchanged: il caffè → i caffè.
Nouns in -co/-go/-ca/-ga often add h to keep the hard sound: amico → amici but amica → amiche.
topics.summary: Italian forms plurals by changing the final vowel, not by adding -s.
topics.tip: Don't add -s: 'pizzas' is wrong; say 'due pizze'.
topics.title: Plurals

rules: Adjectives in -o have four forms: alto, alta, alti, alte; those in -e have two: grande, grandi.
Most adjectives follow the noun: 'una casa grande'.
Common short adjectives (bello, buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio, giovane, bravo) can come before the noun.
Colors and nationalities follow the noun and agree with it.
topics.summary: Adjectives describe nouns and must match them in gender and number. They usually come after the noun.
topics.tip: English puts adjectives first ('red car'); in Italian say 'macchina rossa'.
topics.title: Adjectives: Agreement & Position

rules: Pronouns: io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro.
Use 'tu' for friends, family and children; use formal 'Lei' (with third-person singular verb) for strangers, elders and professionals.
Omit the pronoun unless you need emphasis or contrast.
Formal 'Lei' is often written with a capital L to distinguish it from 'she'.
topics.summary: Subject pronouns (I, you, he...) are often dropped because the verb ending shows who is acting. Italian has an informal and a formal 'you'.
topics.tip: Don't say 'Io sono...' every time; it sounds emphatic. Just use the verb: 'Sono americano.'
topics.title: Subject Pronouns & Formal 'You'

rules: -are (parlare): parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano.
-ere (vendere): vendo, vendi, vende, vendiamo, vendete, vendono.
-ire (dormire): dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono; some -ire verbs add -isc- (finire: finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono).
The present also expresses 'I am doing' and near future plans.
topics.summary: Italian verbs fall into three groups by infinitive ending: -are, -ere, -ire. You drop the ending and add one that matches the subject.
topics.tip: There is no separate '-ing' form: 'I am eating' is simply 'mangio'.
topics.title: Regular Present Tense

examples.de: We are going to the beach.

rules: essere (to be): sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono.
avere (to have): ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno.
andare (to go): vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno; fare (to do/make): faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.
Also learn volere (want), potere (can), dovere (must), venire (come), dare (give).
topics.summary: The most common verbs are irregular, so learn them early. They are essential for everyday communication.
topics.tip: Italian uses 'avere' for age and many feelings: 'Ho trent'anni', 'Ho freddo' (I am cold), not 'sono'.
topics.title: Essential Irregular Verbs

rules: Form the participle: -are → -ato, -ere → -uto, -ire → -ito (parlato, venduto, dormito).
Most verbs use avere: 'ho mangiato'.
Verbs of motion and change, and reflexive verbs, use essere, and the participle agrees with the subject: 'è andata'.
Common irregular participles: fatto, visto, preso, scritto, detto, stato.
topics.summary: The passato prossimo is the main conversational past. It combines a present form of 'avere' or 'essere' with a past participle (the verb form meaning 'done').
topics.tip: One tense covers both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'. Don't forget to match the participle with essere: 'Maria è stata', 'Marco è stato'.
topics.title: Past Tense (Passato Prossimo)

examples.de: When I was little, I played outside.

rules: Imperfect (-are/-ere/-ire): parlavo, parlavi, parlava, parlavamo, parlavate, parlavano (similar pattern with -ev-/-iv-).
Use imperfect for 'used to', descriptions and ongoing states; use passato prossimo for completed events.
Future: drop the final -e of the infinitive and add -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno (-are verbs change to -er-: parlerò).
In casual speech, the present is often used for the near future.
topics.summary: The imperfect describes ongoing or habitual past actions and background. The future is formed with its own endings.
topics.tip: Choose by meaning: 'Ero stanco' (I was tired, as a state) versus 'Sono stato in Italia' (I have been to Italy, as an event).
topics.title: Imperfect & Future

rules: Put 'non' directly before the verb: 'Non capisco.'
Double negatives are normal: 'Non vedo nessuno', 'Non ho niente', 'Non vado mai'.
Yes/no questions keep statement word order; only the intonation rises.
Question words: chi (who), che/cosa (what), dove (where), quando (when), come (how), perché (why/because), quanto (how much).
topics.summary: Making sentences negative or asking questions is simple in Italian, with little change in word order.
topics.tip: There is no 'do/does' helper in Italian: say 'Parli inglese?', not 'Do you parli...'.
topics.title: Negation & Questions

examples.de: The keys are on the table.
We are having dinner at Marco's.

rules: Key prepositions: di (of/from), a (to/at), da (from/at someone's), in (in), con (with), su (on), per (for), tra/fra (between).
a, di, da, in, su combine with 'the': a+il = al, di+la = della, in+i = nei, su+le = sulle.
Use 'a' with cities and 'in' with countries: 'a Roma', 'in Italia'.
'Da' also means 'at someone's place': 'da Marco'.
topics.summary: Prepositions (small words like 'to', 'in', 'from') often merge with the definite article. Use these merged forms constantly.
topics.tip: Don't say 'a il' or 'di la'; always contract: 'al', 'della'. 'Con' is usually left uncontracted.
topics.title: Prepositions & Contractions

rules: Direct objects: mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le; indirect: mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, gli.
Place them before the verb: 'Lo vedo'; attach to infinitives: 'Voglio vederlo'.
Reflexive verbs use mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si: 'mi chiamo', 'ti alzi'.
Possessives (mio, tuo, suo...) normally take the article and agree with the noun: 'la mia casa'.
topics.summary: Object pronouns and reflexive verbs (verbs where the action returns to the subject) go before the conjugated verb. The basic order is subject–verb–object, but it is flexible.
topics.tip: Don't put the pronoun after the verb as in English ('I see him'); in Italian it goes first: 'Lo vedo'. Family singular nouns drop the article: 'mia sorella', but 'la mia casa'.
topics.title: Pronouns, Reflexives & Word Order

items.expl: Toasted rustic bread rubbed with garlic and topped with diced fresh tomatoes, basil, salt and olive oil. Served as a simple, light starter.
items.name: Bruschetta al pomodoro

items.expl: Thin slices of salty dry-cured ham served with sweet, ripe cantaloupe melon. A classic summer starter.
items.name: Prosciutto crudo e melone

items.expl: Sliced fresh tomatoes and mozzarella layered with basil and olive oil. Served cold.
items.name: Caprese

items.expl: A mixed platter of cured meats, cheeses, marinated vegetables and olives. Contents vary by region and restaurant.
items.name: Antipasto misto

items.expl: Paper-thin slices of raw beef dressed with olive oil, lemon, arugula and shavings of Parmigiano.
items.name: Carpaccio di manzo

items.expl: Cold sliced roast veal covered with a creamy tuna, mayonnaise and caper sauce. A classic from Piedmont.
items.name: Vitello tonnato

items.expl: A fresh cheese pouch with a soft, creamy center, from Puglia, served with cherry tomatoes and olive oil.
items.name: Burrata con pomodorini

items.expl: Fried Sicilian rice balls coated in breadcrumbs, typically filled with ragù and peas or with ham and cheese.
items.name: Arancini

items.expl: A mix of lightly battered, deep-fried squid, shrimp and small fish. Served hot with lemon.
items.name: Fritto misto di mare

items.expl: A cold salad of cooked squid, octopus, shrimp and mussels dressed with olive oil, lemon, parsley and garlic.
items.name: Insalata di mare

items.expl: Roman fried rice croquettes with tomato sauce and a core of melting mozzarella, which stretches like a telephone cord.
items.name: Supplì

items.expl: A thick vegetable soup with beans, potatoes, carrots, celery and often small pasta or rice. Served hot or lukewarm.
items.name: Minestrone

items.expl: A Tuscan soup of stale bread, cannellini beans, kale and other vegetables, reboiled until very thick.
items.name: Ribollita

items.expl: A Roman broth with beaten egg and Parmigiano stirred in to form small ribbons. Light and comforting.
items.name: Stracciatella alla romana

items.expl: Small toasted bread slices topped with a warm, rich chicken liver spread. A traditional Tuscan appetizer.
items.name: Crostini toscani

items.expl: Oven-roasted potatoes, usually with rosemary, garlic and olive oil. Crispy outside and soft inside.
items.name: Patate al forno

items.expl: A simple mixed green salad with lettuce, tomato, carrot and sometimes cucumber. Dressed at the table with oil, vinegar and salt.
items.name: Insalata mista

items.expl: Spinach sautéed in olive oil with garlic, sometimes with a little chili. Often ordered with meat dishes.
items.name: Spinaci saltati

items.expl: Grilled slices of eggplant dressed with olive oil, garlic and parsley. Served warm or at room temperature.
items.name: Melanzane alla griglia

items.expl: Grilled seasonal vegetables such as zucchini, peppers and eggplant, drizzled with olive oil.
items.name: Verdure grigliate

items.expl: Bitter chicory or wild greens boiled, then pan-fried with garlic, olive oil and chili. A Roman and southern classic.
items.name: Cicoria ripassata

items.expl: Tuscan cannellini beans stewed in tomato sauce with garlic and sage.
items.name: Fagioli all'uccelletto

items.expl: A stew of bell peppers slowly cooked with onions, tomatoes and olive oil. Served warm or cold.
items.name: Peperonata

items.expl: Roman pasta with egg yolks, Pecorino Romano, crispy guanciale (cured pork cheek) and black pepper. The heat of the pasta turns the egg into a creamy sauce, with no cream added.
items.name: Spaghetti alla carbonara

items.expl: Thick, hollow pasta in a sauce of tomato, guanciale (cured pork cheek) and Pecorino Romano, often with a touch of chili. A classic from Amatrice, now served all over Rome.
items.name: Bucatini all'amatriciana

items.expl: Simple Roman pasta with Pecorino Romano and lots of black pepper. The cheese is melted with a little pasta water into a creamy sauce.
items.name: Spaghetti cacio e pepe

items.expl: Roman pasta with guanciale (cured pork cheek), Pecorino Romano and black pepper. It is like amatriciana without the tomato.
items.name: Rigatoni alla gricia

items.expl: Fresh egg pasta ribbons with a slow-cooked meat sauce of beef and pork, tomato, soffritto and often a little wine. This is the real "Bolognese" from Emilia-Romagna.
items.name: Tagliatelle al ragù

items.expl: Baked layers of egg pasta sheets, ragù, béchamel and Parmigiano Reggiano. Served as a hot, sliceable square with a golden crust.
items.name: Lasagne alla bolognese

items.expl: Spaghetti tossed with fresh clams in their shells, garlic, olive oil, white wine and parsley. Usually has no tomato, and sometimes a little chili.
items.name: Spaghetti alle vongole

items.expl: Twisted Ligurian pasta with a sauce of basil, pine nuts, Parmigiano, Pecorino and olive oil. It is often served with potatoes and green beans.
items.name: Pesto alla genovese (Trofie al pesto)

items.expl: Sicilian pasta with tomato sauce, fried aubergine (eggplant), basil and salted ricotta salata. Named after Bellini's opera.
items.name: Pasta alla Norma

items.expl: Quick pasta with garlic gently fried in olive oil, chili flakes and parsley. A favorite late-night dish.
items.name: Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino

items.expl: Penne in a spicy tomato sauce with garlic and plenty of chili. "Arrabbiata" means "angry".
items.name: Penne all'arrabbiata

items.expl: Small ear-shaped pasta from Puglia with bitter turnip greens, garlic, chili and often anchovies. Sometimes topped with toasted breadcrumbs.
items.name: Orecchiette alle cime di rapa

items.expl: Potato dumplings baked in tomato sauce with mozzarella and basil. Served bubbling hot from the oven.
items.name: Gnocchi alla sorrentina

items.expl: Creamy risotto colored golden with saffron, made with butter, stock and Parmigiano. Traditionally served with ossobuco.
items.name: Risotto alla milanese

items.expl: Creamy rice cooked slowly with porcini mushrooms, stock, onion, butter and Parmigiano. A rich autumn dish.
items.name: Risotto ai funghi porcini

items.expl: Neapolitan pizza with tomato sauce, fresh mozzarella, basil and olive oil. Its red, white and green colors echo the Italian flag.
items.name: Pizza Margherita

items.expl: Pizza with tomato, mozzarella and spicy salame piccante. Sometimes also has chili oil.
items.name: Pizza Diavola

items.expl: White or tomato-based pizza topped with four cheeses, typically mozzarella, gorgonzola, fontina and Parmigiano. Rich and creamy.
items.name: Pizza Quattro Formaggi

items.expl: Thin veal cutlet on the bone, breaded and fried in butter until golden. Served with a lemon wedge.
items.name: Cotoletta alla milanese

items.expl: Cross-cut veal shank braised slowly with white wine, broth and vegetables until tender. Usually served with risotto alla milanese.
items.name: Ossobuco alla milanese

items.expl: Thin veal slices topped with prosciutto and sage, pan-fried and finished with white wine and butter. The name means "jumps in the mouth".
items.name: Saltimbocca alla romana

items.expl: Thick T-bone steak from Tuscany, grilled over charcoal and served rare with salt, olive oil and lemon. Sold by weight and usually shared.
items.name: Bistecca alla fiorentina

items.expl: Boneless pork roasted whole with garlic, fennel, rosemary and plenty of salt, with crisp skin. Often sold in slices or in a bread roll at markets.
items.name: Porchetta

items.expl: Baked layers of fried aubergine (eggplant), tomato sauce, mozzarella and Parmigiano. A staple of southern Italy, served warm or at room temperature.
items.name: Parmigiana di melanzane

items.expl: Lightly floured and fried squid and prawns, served hot with lemon. A popular seaside dish.
items.name: Frittura di calamari e gamberi

items.expl: A creamy whipped spread of salt cod, olive oil and sometimes milk, typical of Venice. Served on grilled polenta or toasted bread as a snack or appetizer.
items.name: Baccalà mantecato

items.expl: Sicilian stuffed sardines filled with breadcrumbs, pine nuts, raisins and herbs, then rolled and baked or fried. Often served warm or at room temperature as a starter.
items.name: Sarde a beccafico

items.expl: Grilled swordfish steak, usually dressed with olive oil, lemon and herbs. A classic main course in Sicily and southern Italy.
items.name: Spada alla griglia

items.expl: Whole sea bass baked in the oven with olive oil, herbs, lemon and often potatoes. Usually presented whole and filleted at the table.
items.name: Branzino al forno

items.expl: Sea bream gently poached in a light broth of water, cherry tomatoes, garlic, parsley and olive oil. A light, fresh dish from Campania.
items.name: Orata all'acqua pazza

items.expl: Venetian fried sardines marinated in sweet and sour onions, vinegar, raisins and pine nuts. Served cold as an appetizer.
items.name: Sarde in saor

items.expl: Mussels steamed open in white wine with garlic, parsley and olive oil, sometimes with tomato. Eaten with bread to soak up the juices.
items.name: Cozze alla marinara

items.expl: Mussels cooked in their own juices with lots of black pepper, garlic and lemon. A Neapolitan seafood classic.
items.name: Impepata di cozze

items.expl: Tender octopus boiled then grilled, usually served with olive oil, lemon and parsley. Often accompanied by potatoes.
items.name: Polpo alla griglia

items.expl: Whole prawns grilled in their shells with olive oil, garlic and lemon. Eaten with your hands.
items.name: Gamberi alla griglia

items.expl: Sardinian pasta with grated cured mullet roe, olive oil, garlic and sometimes lemon zest. Salty, savory and rich in flavor.
items.name: Spaghetti alla bottarga

items.expl: Tuna preserved in olive oil, sold in jars or tins in every supermarket. Eaten in salads, sandwiches, on pasta or as an appetizer.
items.name: Tonno sott'olio

items.expl: A small folded pizza dough pocket, typically filled with tomato and mozzarella, then deep-fried. Popular in Puglia and sold hot from street stands.
items.name: Panzerotto

items.expl: A thin flatbread from Romagna, folded around fillings like prosciutto, squacquerone cheese and rocket. Sold at kiosks and cafés.
items.name: Piadina romagnola

items.expl: A crusty roll filled with sliced roast pork seasoned with herbs and garlic. A common market and roadside snack.
items.name: Panino con la porchetta

items.expl: A sandwich of soft bread filled with thinly sliced mortadella, the Bolognese pork cold cut. Sometimes with pistachios or cheese.
items.name: Panino con la mortadella

items.expl: Rectangular pizza baked in large trays and sold by weight in slices. Toppings range from simple tomato to potatoes or cured meats.
items.name: Pizza al taglio

items.expl: A Neapolitan fried pizza pocket filled with ricotta, salami and tomato or mozzarella. Crisp outside and soft inside.
items.name: Pizza fritta

items.expl: Soft, oily Ligurian flatbread with dimples, olive oil and coarse salt. Eaten at breakfast or as a snack, often dipped in cappuccino.
items.name: Focaccia genovese

items.expl: A Florentine sandwich of slow-cooked cow's fourth stomach in a roll, often with green sauce or spicy sauce. Sold from street carts.
items.name: Lampredotto

items.expl: Sicilian fritters made from chickpea flour, fried until crisp. Often eaten in a sesame roll with a squeeze of lemon.
items.name: Panelle

items.expl: Fried potato croquettes, often with mozzarella or ham inside. A Neapolitan street snack sold in paper cones.
items.name: Crocchè di patate

items.expl: Large green olives stuffed with seasoned meat, breaded and deep-fried. A specialty of Ascoli Piceno in Le Marche.
items.name: Olive all'ascolana

items.expl: Soft, crustless triangular white bread sandwich with fillings like tuna, egg, mayonnaise, ham or vegetables. Found in bars throughout Italy.
items.name: Tramezzino

items.expl: Layered dessert of coffee-soaked savoiardi biscuits and a cream of mascarpone, eggs and sugar, dusted with cocoa. Served chilled, usually in a square slice or a glass.
items.name: Tiramisù

items.expl: Soft, wobbly set cream dessert made from cream, sugar and gelatin. Usually served with berry sauce, caramel or chocolate.
items.name: Panna cotta

items.expl: Crisp fried pastry tube filled with sweetened ricotta, often with chocolate chips or candied fruit. Filled to order so the shell stays crunchy.
items.name: Cannolo siciliano

items.expl: Sicilian sponge cake layered with sweet ricotta, covered in marzipan and icing and decorated with candied fruit. Very sweet and colorful.
items.name: Cassata siciliana

items.expl: Italian ice cream, denser and softer than American ice cream, served in a cone (cono) or cup (coppetta). Choose from flavors like pistacchio, nocciola, stracciatella and fior di latte.
items.name: Gelato

items.expl: Warm, frothy custard whisked from egg yolks, sugar and sweet Marsala wine. Eaten with a spoon or served with biscuits.
items.name: Zabaione

items.expl: Hard, twice-baked almond biscuits from Tuscany. Traditionally dunked in Vin Santo dessert wine.
items.name: Cantucci

items.expl: A scoop of vanilla or fior di latte gelato "drowned" in a hot shot of espresso. Eaten as a dessert with a spoon.
items.name: Affogato al caffè

items.expl: Shortcrust tart filled with lemony pastry cream and topped with pine nuts and powdered sugar. A classic Tuscan grandmother's cake.
items.name: Torta della nonna

items.expl: Neapolitan pastry with many thin, crisp layers shaped like a shell. Filled with sweet ricotta, semolina and candied orange peel.
items.name: Sfogliatella

items.expl: Small, soft yeast cake from Naples soaked in rum syrup. Sold plain or filled with cream.
items.name: Babà

items.expl: Tall, fluffy Milanese yeast cake with raisins and candied citrus peel, traditionally eaten at Christmas. Sold in large boxes in supermarkets and bakeries.
items.name: Panettone

items.expl: Italian breakfast croissant, softer and sweeter than the French one. Ask for it vuoto (plain), alla crema, alla marmellata (jam) or al cioccolato.
items.name: Cornetto

items.expl: Soft, slightly sweet Roman bun split and filled with a generous amount of whipped cream. Popular for breakfast in Rome.
items.name: Maritozzo con la panna

items.expl: Fried doughnut without a hole, rolled in sugar and often filled with custard, chocolate or jam. Also called krapfen in the north.
items.name: Bombolone

items.expl: Crisp, dry toasted bread slices sold in packs at supermarkets. Eaten at breakfast with jam or hazelnut spread.
items.name: Fette biscottate

items.expl: Thin, crunchy breadsticks from Turin. Often placed on the table as a bread substitute or eaten with cured ham.
items.name: Grissini

items.expl: Small, ring-shaped crunchy snacks from southern Italy made with flour, olive oil and white wine. Plain, with fennel seeds or with chili.
items.name: Taralli

items.expl: Flat Tuscan bread similar to focaccia, crisp outside and glossy with olive oil and coarse salt. Eaten plain or split and filled as a sandwich.
items.name: Schiacciata all'olio

items.expl: Shortcrust tart with a jam filling and a lattice top. Sold by the slice or whole at bakeries and eaten for breakfast or a snack.
items.name: Crostata alla marmellata

items.expl: Bright orange aperitivo of Aperol, prosecco and a splash of soda, served over ice with an orange slice. Typically drunk before dinner with snacks.
items.name: Spritz Aperol

items.expl: Strong, bitter cocktail of gin, Campari and sweet red vermouth, served over ice with an orange slice.
items.name: Negroni

items.expl: Sweet, strong lemon liqueur from southern Italy, served ice-cold in small glasses after a meal.
items.name: Limoncello

items.expl: Strong, clear spirit distilled from grape pomace. Sipped after a meal as a digestivo.
items.name: Grappa

items.expl: Bitter herbal liqueur, such as Montenegro or Averna, drunk after dinner to aid digestion. Served neat or over ice.
items.name: Amaro

items.expl: Dry to off-dry sparkling white wine from the Veneto region. Ordered by the glass (calice) as an aperitivo or for toasts. Grape varieties: mainly Glera (at least 85%), with up to 15% of other permitted varieties such as Pinot Noir, Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay or Verdiso.
items.name: Prosecco

items.expl: Dark, bittersweet soft drink made from the chinotto citrus fruit. Sold in small bottles at bars and supermarkets.
items.name: Chinotto

items.expl: Freshly squeezed orange juice made to order at bars. In Sicily, blood oranges (arance rosse) are often used.
items.name: Spremuta d'arancia

items.expl: A single short, intense espresso served in a small cup, drunk standing at the bar at any time of day. Achtung: if you ask for just 'coffee' or 'un caffè', you get an espresso, not a large filter or drip coffee as in the US or UK.
items.name: Caffè

items.expl: An espresso made with more water, so it is a bit larger and milder but still served in a small cup. Achtung: it is not the same as an Americano or a long black; it is still only about 40-50 ml.
items.name: Caffè lungo

items.expl: A very concentrated espresso made with less water, so it is stronger, thicker and only a few sips. Often ordered by locals after a meal or in the morning.
items.name: Caffè ristretto

items.expl: Espresso with steamed milk and a thick layer of foam in a medium cup, about 150-180 ml. Italians drink it only at breakfast or until about 11 am, and ordering one after a meal is seen as odd. Achtung: it is smaller and less foamy-heavy than the huge versions abroad, and it is not served with chocolate sprinkles unless you ask.
items.name: Cappuccino

items.expl: An espresso 'stained' with a small dash of milk foam, served in a small cup. Drunk any time of day when you want a softer espresso. Achtung: it is not the large layered caramel macchiato known from coffee chains in English-speaking countries.
items.name: Caffè macchiato

items.expl: A tall glass of warm milk 'stained' with a shot of espresso, with a layer of foam on top and mild in taste. Mostly a breakfast or morning drink. Achtung: if you just order 'latte' in Italy, you get a glass of plain milk, not a coffee.
items.name: Latte macchiato

items.expl: Espresso mixed with a lot of hot milk and little foam, served in a large cup or glass. Typically a home or breakfast drink and milder than a cappuccino. Achtung: it is not the same as a 'latte' in English-speaking countries, and asking only for 'latte' gets you plain milk.
items.name: Caffellatte

items.expl: A small glass with cocoa powder, a shot of espresso and milk foam, often dusted with more cocoa. A sweet, creamy pick-me-up popular in northern Italy, especially in Piedmont, at any time of day.
items.name: Marocchino

items.expl: An espresso served with hot water added, or with a cup of hot water on the side, giving a larger, milder drink. Found in bars but not very typical for Italians. Achtung: it is not the same as drip or filter coffee, and it tastes lighter than a normal espresso.
items.name: Caffè americano

items.expl: An espresso 'corrected' with a splash of liquor, usually grappa, sambuca or brandy, served in a small cup. Often ordered after a meal or in the morning by some locals. Achtung: this contains alcohol, so be aware if you are driving.
items.name: Caffè corretto

items.expl: Espresso shaken hard with ice and sugar until frothy and then poured into a chilled cocktail glass. A refreshing, strong summer drink, often drunk in the afternoon or after lunch. Achtung: it is not a milkshake, and unlike iced coffee abroad it is small and very strong.
items.name: Caffè shakerato

items.expl: A caffeine-free hot drink made from roasted barley, served in a cup like an espresso or with milk as 'orzo grande'. Popular with children, in the evening, or for people avoiding caffeine. Achtung: it looks like coffee but contains no coffee, and it is not the same as barley tea.
items.name: Caffè d'orzo

items.expl: A pale golden lager, crisp and lightly bitter, around 4.6% ABV. Found in almost every bar and restaurant; order a 'piccola' (about 20 cl), 'media' (about 40 cl) or a bottle.
items.name: Birra Moretti

items.expl: A light, refreshing pilsner-style lager with a mild hop note, about 5.1% ABV. Served cold in bottles or on tap at bars, pizzerias and beach clubs.
items.name: Peroni Nastro Azzurro

items.expl: A golden lager from Piedmont with a balanced malty taste and gentle bitterness, about 4.8% ABV. Popular in northern Italy, often with pizza or aperitivo snacks.
items.name: Menabrea Bionda

items.expl: A Sardinian pale lager, light and slightly malty, about 4.7% ABV. The unfiltered 'Ichnusa Non Filtrata' is cloudier and fuller in flavor; a classic beach drink in Sardinia.
items.name: Birra Ichnusa

items.expl: A Sicilian lager, golden and easy-drinking, about 4.4% ABV. The 'Messina Cristalli di Sale' version is brewed with sea salt and is popular in summer.
items.name: Birra Messina

items.expl: A South Tyrolean lager brewed in the Alps, clean, crisp and slightly hoppy, about 4.8% ABV. Common in Alpine regions and served in tall glasses or half-liter mugs.
items.name: Birra Forst

items.expl: A golden lager with a soft malt character and light bitterness, about 4.8% ABV. Widely available in northern Italy; the 'Poretti 4 Luppoli' version is more aromatic with four hop varieties.
items.name: Birra Poretti

items.expl: Italian craft beer from small independent breweries, in styles such as IPA, amber ale or saison, usually 5-8% ABV. Look for it at a 'birrificio' or pub, often served in 20 cl, 40 cl or 50 cl glasses.
items.name: Birra artigianale

items.expl: A well-known craft beer from Piedmont, amber-golden with a fruity, spicy flavor, brewed with Italian grains, about 6.5% ABV. Served in bottles at craft beer bars and good restaurants.
items.name: Baladin Nazionale

items.expl: Draft beer, which is what you ask for when you want it from the tap. Order a 'piccola' (about 20 cl), 'media' (about 40 cl) or 'grande' (about 50 cl), usually a lager of about 4.5-5%.
items.name: Birra alla spina

items.expl: A dry red from the heart of Tuscany, with cherry fruit, good acidity and firm tannins. Made mainly from Sangiovese (at least 80%), sometimes with Canaiolo or Cabernet; great with pasta with meat sauce, grilled meat and pizza.
items.name: Chianti Classico

items.expl: A powerful, dry red from Piedmont known for tannins, rose and tar aromas and long aging. Made entirely from Nebbiolo; drink it with braised meat, truffle dishes and aged cheese.
items.name: Barolo

items.expl: A full-bodied, dry red from Tuscany with dark cherry, spice and a long finish. Made 100% from Sangiovese (locally called Brunello); pairs well with steak, game and aged pecorino.
items.name: Brunello di Montalcino

items.expl: A soft, fruity, dry red from Abruzzo with plum and blackberry flavors and gentle tannins. Made from Montepulciano grapes; an everyday wine for pasta, grilled meats and pizza.
items.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo

items.expl: A dry, rich red from the Veneto, with cherry and spice and a slightly raisiny depth. Mainly Corvina, with Corvinone and Rondinella, refermented on Amarone pomace; good with roasts and risotto.
items.name: Valpolicella Ripasso

items.expl: A very full, dry and intense red from the Veneto, with dried fruit, chocolate and high alcohol (15% or more). Made from partially dried Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella grapes; drink with game, stews and strong cheese.
items.name: Amarone della Valpolicella

items.expl: A ripe, dry to off-dry red from Puglia with jammy dark fruit and warm spice. Made from Primitivo grapes; goes with grilled meat, orecchiette with ragù and hearty dishes.
items.name: Primitivo di Manduria

items.expl: A light, dry, crisp white from northeastern Italy with pear and citrus notes. Made from Pinot Grigio; a popular choice with seafood, salads and as an aperitif.
items.name: Pinot Grigio delle Venezie

items.expl: A dry, fresh white from Sardinia with citrus, herbal and slightly salty notes. Made from Vermentino grapes; excellent with grilled fish, shellfish and seafood pasta.
items.name: Vermentino di Sardegna

items.expl: A dry, delicate white from the Veneto with almond, apple and mineral notes. Made mainly from Garganega (at least 70%), often with Trebbiano di Soave; pairs well with risotto, fish and light starters.
items.name: Soave Classico

items.expl: A dry sparkling wine from Lombardy made by the traditional bottle-fermentation method, with fine bubbles and brioche notes. Made from Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and sometimes Pinot Bianco; served as an aperitif or with seafood.
items.name: Franciacorta

items.expl: A sweet dessert wine from Tuscany with notes of dried apricot, honey and nuts. Made from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia grapes (red Sangiovese in the Occhio di Pernice style); typically served with almond biscuits called cantucci.
items.name: Vin Santo

rules: c und g vor e/i klingen weich ("tsch" und "dsch"): cena, gelato.
c und g vor a/o/u sowie ch/gh vor e/i klingen hart ("k" und "g"): casa, che, spaghetti.
gn klingt wie "nj" (gnocchi), sc vor e/i wie "sch" (pesce), gli wie "lj" (famiglia).
Doppelte Konsonanten werden deutlich länger gesprochen; meist betont man die vorletzte Silbe.
topics.summary: Italienisch wird fast so gesprochen, wie es geschrieben wird. Wenige Buchstabenkombinationen verdienen besondere Aufmerksamkeit.
topics.tip: Doppelkonsonanten wirklich lang sprechen: "pena" (Kummer) und "penna" (Stift) sind verschiedene Wörter. Das h ist immer stumm: hotel klingt wie "otel".
topics.title: Aussprache & Betonung

rules: Männlich: il (vor den meisten Konsonanten), lo (vor s+Konsonant, z, gn, ps), l' (vor Vokal).
Weiblich: la (vor Konsonant), l' (vor Vokal).
Unbestimmt: un, uno (männlich), una, un' (weiblich).
Die meisten Wörter auf -o sind männlich, auf -a weiblich; -e kann beides sein.
topics.summary: Jedes Nomen ist männlich oder weiblich. Der Artikel (Begleiter wie "der/die/das" oder "ein/eine") richtet sich danach und nach dem Anfangslaut des Wortes.
topics.tip: Das Geschlecht stimmt oft nicht mit dem Deutschen überein: das Meer (neutral) heißt il mare, die Milch heißt il latte. Lerne Nomen immer mit Artikel.
topics.title: Artikel & Geschlecht

rules: -o wird zu -i, -a wird zu -e, -e wird zu -i.
Die Artikel ändern sich: il → i, lo/l' (m.) → gli, la/l' (w.) → le.
Wörter auf Betonungsvokal (città, caffè) und Kurzwörter (film, bar) bleiben gleich.
Endungen auf -co/-go/-ca/-ga verändern oft die Aussprache: amico → amici, amica → amiche.
topics.summary: Der Plural wird meist durch Wechsel der Endung gebildet, nicht durch Anhängen eines -s.
topics.tip: Nicht -s anhängen wie im Englischen: Es heißt due pizze, nicht "due pizzas". Der Pizza-Plural im Deutschen ist kein Vorbild.
topics.title: Plural

rules: Adjektive auf -o haben vier Formen: rosso, rossa, rossi, rosse.
Adjektive auf -e haben zwei Formen: grande, grandi.
Die meisten Adjektive stehen nach dem Nomen: una casa grande.
Einige häufige Adjektive (bello, buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo) stehen oft davor, dann ändert sich manchmal die Bedeutung oder Form.
topics.summary: Adjektive (Eigenschaftswörter) passen sich in Geschlecht und Zahl an das Nomen an und stehen meist dahinter.
topics.tip: Typischer Fehler: das Adjektiv vor das Nomen setzen wie im Deutschen. Farben und Nationalitäten kommen fast immer danach.
topics.title: Adjektive: Angleichung & Stellung

rules: Formen: io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro.
Das Pronomen nutzt man nur zur Betonung oder Klarstellung.
Höflich siezt man mit "Lei" und der 3. Person Singular des Verbs.
Informell duzt man mit "tu", Mehrzahl sowohl formell als auch informell "voi".
topics.summary: Personalpronomen (ich, du, er …) werden im Italienischen meist weggelassen, weil die Verbendung die Person schon zeigt. Es gibt eine eigene Höflichkeitsform.
topics.tip: Nicht ständig "io" sagen, das klingt betont. Beim Siezen: Lei plus 3. Person Singular, nicht die 3. Person Plural wie im Deutschen ("Sie").
topics.title: Personalpronomen & Höflichkeitsform

rules: -are (parlare): parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano.
-ere (vendere): vendo, vendi, vende, vendiamo, vendete, vendono.
-ire (dormire): dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono.
Einige -ire-Verben (capire, finire) fügen -isc- ein: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono.
topics.summary: Italienische Verben enden im Infinitiv auf -are, -ere oder -ire. Die Endung wechselt je nach Person.
topics.tip: Das Präsens dient auch für die nahe Zukunft: Domani parto = Morgen reise ich ab. Für "gerade eben" gibt es zusätzlich stare + Gerundium: sto mangiando.
topics.title: Verben im Präsens (regelmäßig)

rules: essere (sein): sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono.
avere (haben): ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno.
andare (gehen): vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno.
fare (machen): faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno; ebenso wichtig: volere, potere, dovere.
topics.summary: Einige sehr häufige Verben folgen eigenen Mustern und müssen auswendig gelernt werden.
topics.tip: Das h in ho, hai, ha, hanno ist stumm, unterscheidet aber Schriftbild: o (oder) und ho (ich habe), a (zu) und ha (er hat). Höflicher als voglio ist vorrei (ich möchte).
topics.title: Die wichtigsten unregelmäßigen Verben

rules: Hilfsverb ist avere (meist) oder essere (bei Bewegung und Zustandsänderung, z. B. andare, venire, partire).
Partizip: -are → -ato, -ere → -uto, -ire → -ito (parlato, venduto, dormito).
Mit essere passt sich das Partizip an das Subjekt an: lei è andata, loro sono andati.
Wichtige unregelmäßige Partizipien: fatto, preso, visto, stato, detto.
topics.summary: Das passato prossimo ist die wichtigste Vergangenheitsform im Alltag. Sie wird aus einem Hilfsverb und dem Partizip Perfekt (Mittelwort der Vergangenheit) gebildet.
topics.tip: Das Hilfsverb entspricht nicht immer dem Deutschen: Ich bin gewesen heißt "sono stato", aber "ich habe gewohnt" heißt "ho abitato". Prüfe bei Bewegung die Angleichung des Partizips.
topics.title: Vergangenheit (passato prossimo)

examples.de: Wo ist er? Er wird wohl im Büro sein.

rules: -are wird zu -er-: parlerò, parlerai, parlerà, parleremo, parlerete, parleranno.
-ere und -ire behalten ihren Vokal: venderò, dormirò.
Unregelmäßig: essere → sarò, avere → avrò, andare → andrò, fare → farò.
Das Futur drückt auch Vermutung aus: Sarà vero. = Das wird wohl stimmen.
topics.summary: Das einfache Futur wird mit eigenen Endungen am Verbstamm gebildet. Im Alltag nutzt man oft auch das Präsens.
topics.tip: Bei -are-Verben wird das a der Endung zu e: parlare → parlerò. Für Pläne reicht oft das Präsens: Domani vado al mare.
topics.title: Zukunft (futuro semplice)

rules: Einfache Verneinung: non + Verb.
Bei weiteren Verneinungswörtern (niente, nessuno, mai) steht non davor, danach folgt das Wort: Non vedo niente.
Kommt das Verneinungswort vor dem Verb, entfällt non: Nessuno parla.
Pronomen stehen zwischen non und Verb: Non lo so.
topics.summary: Die Verneinung ist einfach: Man setzt non direkt vor das konjugierte Verb.
topics.tip: Doppelte Verneinung ist im Italienischen korrekt und verlangt: non … niente, non … mai. Anders als im Deutschen hebt sie sich nicht auf.
topics.title: Verneinung

examples.de: Warum bist du müde? Weil ich viel gearbeitet habe.
examples.x: Perché sei stanco? Perché ho lavorato molto.

rules: Ja/Nein-Frage: gleiche Wortstellung wie die Aussage, mit steigender Intonation.
Fragewörter: chi (wer), che cosa/cosa (was), dove (wo), quando (wann), come (wie), perché (warum/weil), quanto (wie viel).
Fragewort steht am Satzanfang, das Subjekt oft am Ende.
Perché bedeutet sowohl "warum" als auch "weil".
topics.summary: Fragen bildet man oft ohne Umstellung, nur durch die Satzmelodie. Dazu kommen die gängigen Fragewörter.
topics.tip: Nicht wie im Deutschen das Verb vor das Subjekt stellen. Statt "Sprichst du?" sagt man einfach "Parli?" mit Fragemelodie.
topics.title: Fragen

examples.de: Das ist das Auto von Marco.

rules: Wichtig: a (zu/in/an), di (von), da (von/bei/seit), in (in), su (auf), con (mit), per (für).
Mit bestimmtem Artikel verschmelzen di, a, da, in, su: a + il = al, di + la = della, in + lo = nello.
Städte: a (a Roma); Länder: in (in Italia); Personen: da (da Marco).
Grundstellung: Subjekt – Verb – Objekt; Objektpronomen stehen vor dem Verb: Lo vedo.
topics.summary: Präpositionen (Verhältniswörter) verschmelzen oft mit dem Artikel. Die Satzstellung ist meist Subjekt – Verb – Objekt.
topics.tip: Verschmelzungen wie al, nel, sul sind Pflicht, man kann nicht "a il" sagen. Und "zu jemandem" heißt da: Vado dal medico (zum Arzt), nicht "a il medico".
topics.title: Präpositionen & Satzbau

docs.expl: Heiße Milch mit Milchschaum und einem Schuss Espresso, im hohen Glas serviert. Er ist mild und eher ein Frühstücksgetränk.

forms.t: Vorrei **un** latte macchiato, per favore.
Scusi, potrei avere **un** latte macchiato, per cortesia?

docs.name: Latte macchiato

rules: Las consonantes dobles (tt, ll, zz...) se pronuncian más largas: 'pala' no es 'palla'.
'c' y 'g' son suaves ante e/i (ce = 'che', gi = 'yi' fuerte) y duras ante a/o/u o con h (che = 'ke', ghi = 'gui').
'gn' suena como la ñ, 'gli' como una ll fuerte ('figlio') y 'sc' ante e/i como 'sh' ('pesce').
La 'h' es siempre muda y la 'z' suena como 'ts' o 'dz', no como la z española.
topics.summary: El italiano se pronuncia casi como se escribe. Hay que prestar atención a las consonantes dobles y a algunos grupos de letras.
topics.tip: Error típico: pronunciar la 'c' de 'ciao' como 's' o 'z' española. Se dice 'chao'. Y no te comas las consonantes dobles: 'sete' (sed) ≠ 'sette' (siete).
topics.title: Pronunciación y acentuación

examples.x: Lo studente e lo scarpa... (correcto: la scarpa)

rules: Masculino determinado: il (consonante), lo (s+consonante, z, gn, ps), l' (vocal).
Femenino determinado: la (consonante), l' (vocal).
Indeterminado: un, uno (ante s+consonante o z), una, un' (femenino ante vocal).
Generalmente -o es masculino y -a femenino; -e puede ser de ambos géneros.
topics.summary: Todos los sustantivos son masculinos o femeninos. El artículo cambia según el género y el sonido inicial de la palabra.
topics.tip: Cuidado con las palabras que cambian de género respecto al español: 'il latte' (la leche), 'il sale' (la sal), 'la mano' (la mano, pero terminada en -o). Además, 'lo studente' lleva 'lo', no 'il'.
topics.title: Artículos y género

rules: -o pasa a -i (libro → libri).
-a pasa a -e (casa → case).
-e pasa a -i (nome → nomi), tanto en masculino como en femenino.
Palabras acentuadas o extranjeras no cambian (caffè → caffè, film → film).
topics.summary: El plural se forma cambiando la vocal final, no añadiendo -s como en español.
topics.tip: Error típico: añadir -s ('amicos'). En italiano nunca se forma el plural con -s. Recuerda también: il → i, lo/l' → gli, la → le.
topics.title: El plural

examples.x: Le macchine rosse... (correcto: Le macchine rosse = los coches rojos, 'macchina' es femenino)

rules: Los adjetivos en -o tienen cuatro formas: alto, alta, alti, alte.
Los adjetivos en -e tienen dos: grande, grandi.
Normalmente van detrás del sustantivo; los de uso muy común (bello, buono, grande, piccolo) pueden ir delante.
Colores y nacionalidad siempre van detrás.
topics.summary: Los adjetivos concuerdan en género y número con el sustantivo y normalmente van después de él.
topics.tip: Los posesivos llevan artículo en italiano: 'la mia casa' (mi casa). Excepción: con familiares en singular no se usa ('mia madre').
topics.title: Adjetivos: concordancia y posición

examples.de: Yo soy español y tú eres francés.
examples.x: Io sono spagnolo e tu sei francese.

rules: Pronombres: io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro.
El sujeto se omite salvo para enfatizar o aclarar.
Trato formal singular: 'Lei' con el verbo en tercera persona; informal: 'tu'.
Formal plural: normalmente 'voi'.
topics.summary: El pronombre sujeto suele omitirse, como en español. Para el trato formal se usa 'Lei' (tercera persona singular).
topics.tip: No uses 'tu' con desconocidos mayores o en tiendas y hoteles: usa 'Lei'. No equivale a 'usted' en la forma verbal, pero funciona igual.
topics.title: Pronombres personales y tratamiento formal

examples.x: A che ora finisce il film?

rules: -are (parlare): parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano.
-ere (vendere): vendo, vendi, vende, vendiamo, vendete, vendono.
-ire (dormire): dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono.
Algunos verbos en -ire añaden -isc- (finire: finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono).
topics.summary: Hay tres grupos de verbos según su terminación: -are, -ere e -ire. Se conjugan cambiando la terminación.
topics.tip: Parecido al español pero ojo: la 3ª persona plural acentúa la antepenúltima sílaba ('PARlano', 'VENdono'). Y la 1ª plural siempre es -iamo (no -amos/-emos/-imos).
topics.title: Presente de verbos regulares

examples.de: Soy de Madrid y tengo hambre.
examples.x: Sono di Madrid e ho fame.

rules: Essere: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono.
Avere: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno (la h es muda).
Andare: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno; fare: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.
Volere, potere, dovere: voglio, posso, devo; seguidos de infinitivo.
topics.summary: Algunos verbos muy frecuentes son irregulares y hay que aprenderlos de memoria.
topics.tip: Se usa 'avere' (no 'essere') para hambre, sed, años, frío: 'ho fame', 'ho vent'anni'. Cuidado con 'sono': significa 'soy' y 'son/están'.
topics.title: Verbos irregulares esenciales

rules: Participios regulares: -are → -ato, -ere → -uto, -ire → -ito.
La mayoría de los verbos usa 'avere'; los de movimiento y los reflexivos usan 'essere'.
Con 'essere' el participio concuerda con el sujeto (andato/andata/andati/andate).
Hay participios irregulares frecuentes: fatto, detto, visto, preso, scritto.
topics.summary: Es el pasado más usado en la conversación: auxiliar (avere o essere) más participio pasado.
topics.tip: Error típico: usar siempre 'avere' como en español 'haber'. Con verbos como andare, venire, arrivare, partire, nascere se usa 'essere'. En el sur y en la conversación el passato prossimo también sustituye al indefinido.
topics.title: Pasado próximo (passato prossimo)

rules: -are cambia a -er-: parlare → parlerò, parlerai, parlerà, parleremo, parlerete, parleranno.
-ere e -ire mantienen la vocal: vendere → venderò; dormire → dormirò.
Irregulares comunes: essere → sarò, avere → avrò, andare → andrò, fare → farò.
El futuro también expresa probabilidad: 'Sarà tardi' (Será tarde).
topics.summary: El futuro simple se forma con el infinitivo más terminaciones. En la conversación también se usa el presente para planes cercanos.
topics.tip: Para planes inmediatos es muy natural usar el presente ('Domani parto'), igual que en español 'mañana salgo'. Cuidado con la tilde final: 'parlerò' sí lleva acento, a diferencia del español 'hablaré' que también la lleva, pero la 3ª persona 'parlerà' es aguda.
topics.title: Futuro y formas de expresarlo

examples.x: Non ho mai mangiato il sushi.

rules: 'Non' va directamente antes del verbo conjugado.
Si la palabra negativa va después del verbo, se necesita 'non': non... niente, non... mai, non... nessuno.
Si 'nessuno' o 'niente' van antes del verbo, no se usa 'non'.
En el passato prossimo 'non' va antes del auxiliar.
topics.summary: La negación se forma poniendo 'non' delante del verbo. Con otras palabras negativas, la doble negación es normal.
topics.tip: Igual que en español, la doble negación es correcta. Pero atención: 'no' como respuesta es 'no', y 'non' solo se usa delante de un verbo. No digas 'no parlo'.
topics.title: La negación

rules: Pregunta sí/no: misma frase con entonación ascendente y un solo signo '?'.
Interrogativos: chi, che cosa, dove, quando, come, perché, quanto, quale.
'Quanto' y 'quale' concuerdan con el sustantivo (quanti euro, quale libro).
'Perché' sirve para preguntar (¿por qué?) y para responder (porque).
topics.summary: Las preguntas se forman con la entonación o con palabras interrogativas, sin inversión del sujeto.
topics.tip: No existe el signo de apertura '¿'. Además, no inviertas verbo y sujeto como en inglés: 'Parli italiano?' basta. Cuidado con 'che cosa' vs 'quale': 'Quale vuoi?' (¿cuál quieres?).
topics.title: Preguntas

examples.de: Vivo en Italia desde hace dos años.
examples.x: Vivo in Italia da due anni.

examples.de: Me gusta el café del bar.
examples.x: Mi piace il caffè del bar.

rules: Las preposiciones a, da, di, in, su se unen al artículo: di + il = del, a + la = alla, in + il = nel, su + i = sui.
'A' se usa con ciudades (a Roma) e 'in' con países y regiones (in Spagna).
'Da' indica procedencia, 'da + persona' = a casa de (da Marco), y duración (da due anni).
Los pronombres átonos van antes del verbo: 'Lo vedo', 'Mi piace'.
topics.summary: Las preposiciones se combinan con el artículo (preposiciones articuladas) y el orden básico de la frase es sujeto-verbo-complemento.
topics.tip: Error típico: no contraer la preposición con el artículo ('di il' en lugar de 'del'). Con 'en' + artículo se contrae: 'nel'. Y 'mi piace' funciona como 'me gusta': lo que gusta es el sujeto ('mi piacciono i libri').
topics.title: Preposiciones y orden de la frase
